options: Combines two DataFrames into one using a shared column
Removes duplicate rows from a single DataFrame
Groups rows by a column's value
Converts a DataFrame into a CSV file
questions.explain: merge() combines two separate DataFrames based on a column they share — the Pandas equivalent of a relationship between two tables.

questions.q: What does the 'on' argument in pd.merge(sales, products, on="Product") specify?
options: The shared column both DataFrames are joined on
Which DataFrame appears first in the output
The aggregation to apply after merging
The number of rows to include in the result
questions.explain: on tells Pandas which column to match rows on between the two DataFrames — the same role a key column plays in a Power BI relationship.

questions.q: What is the SQL equivalent of pd.merge()?
options: JOIN
GROUP BY
WHERE
SELECT DISTINCT
questions.explain: pd.merge() is Pandas' name for what SQL calls JOIN — same underlying relational operation, different syntax.

questions.q: What does how="left" keep, compared to how="inner"?
options: Every row from the first (left) table, whether or not it finds a match — inner keeps only rows matching in both tables
Only rows that appear in the second table
how="left" and how="inner" always produce identical results
Every row from both tables regardless of matches, same as inner
questions.explain: left keeps all rows from the first table even without a match (filling missing data as needed); inner keeps only rows with a match in both tables, dropping the rest.

questions.q: How should you decide between how="left" and how="inner" for a specific merge?

Always use "left" regardless of the situation
The choice has no effect on the resulting data
questions.explain: Whether to keep unmatched rows depends on what a missing match actually represents for that data — the same deliberate judgment Lesson 11 taught for missing values.
